hook: GPT-2 is 124 million numbers and one function. Follow a single sentence through it and every shape tells you what happens next.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — GPT-2 is one function from integers to 50,257 scores per position. Follow the shapes and you understand the whole thing.

0:15 QUESTION — This module builds GPT from scratch until it loads OpenAI's real GPT-2 weights and produces the same logits as Hugging Face. Before any component, we need the map: what goes in, what comes out, and the shape at every stop. Every later episode fills in one box on this map.

1:00 INTUITION — Tokens become vectors. Vectors flow up a stack of 12 identical blocks, each one reading from and adding to the same stream. At the top, a final norm and a projection turn each vector into a score for every token in the vocabulary. Position t's scores predict token t+1. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — GPT-2 small: V = 50,257, T_max = 1024, C = d_model = 768, L = 12 layers, nh = 12 heads, hs = C/nh = 64. idx (B, T) int64. x = wte[idx] + wpe[0:T], (B, T, C). Each block: x = x + Attn(LN1(x)); x = x + MLP(LN2(x)), shape stays (B, T, C). Inside attention: q, k, v are (B, nh, T, hs), scores (B, nh, T, T). Inside MLP: (B, T, 4C) = (B, T, 3072). Then LN_f, logits = x W_E^T, (B, T, V). Loss = cross-entropy of logits[:, t] against idx[:, t+1].

6:00 CODE — No model yet. Load GPT2LMHeadModel.from_pretrained('gpt2'). Write trace(model, idx): register_forward_hook on wte, wpe, each h[i], h[i].attn, h[i].mlp, ln_f, lm_head; each hook appends (name, tuple(out.shape)) (taking out[0] if the module returns a tuple). Run on tiktoken gpt2 encoding of 'Hello, I'm a language model,' with B=2. Print the table next to the shapes predicted on the whiteboard.

9:00 RECEIPT — assert logits.shape == (2, T, 50257). For every hooked module, assert the observed shape equals the predicted one from a dict written before running. Parameter count: assert sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) == 124_439_808 (parameters() counts the tied wte/lm_head once).
10:30 MEASURE — The shape trace printed as a vertical table, plus a pie of where the 124.4M parameters live: wte 38.6M, wpe 0.79M, 12 blocks 85.05M, ln_f 1.5k.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — A GPT is embed, L times (x + attn, x + mlp), norm, unembed, and the shape is (B, T, C) the whole way up. Interview line: the only place the T by T interaction happens is attention scores; everything else is per-token.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Token embeddings and the residual stream.

Answer: (B,T) ids -> (B,T,C) embeddings plus positions -> L blocks that keep (B,T,C), with attention internally at (B,nh,T,hs) and (B,nh,T,T) scores and the MLP at (B,T,4C) -> final norm -> (B,T,V) logits, where position t predicts token t+1.
explainer: A GPT takes in a row of integers and returns, for every position, a score for every word it knows.
First, each integer looks up a 768 number vector. Its position looks up another. We add them.
That block flows into the first transformer block. Shape in, B by T by 768. Shape out, the same.
Inside, attention lets positions talk. This is the only place a T by T grid ever appears.
The MLP works on each position alone, widening to 3072 and back down to 768.
Twelve of these blocks stack on top of each other, all writing into the same stream.
At the top, a final norm, then multiply by the embedding table again to get logits over the vocabulary.
The scores at position t are a guess for token t plus one. That is the whole training signal.

hook: Every layer in GPT reads one vector and adds to it. Measure that vector layer by layer and you can watch it think.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Nothing in a transformer overwrites anything. Every layer only adds to one shared vector. Let's measure that vector.

0:15 QUESTION — Anthropic's Transformer Circuits work treats the residual stream as the central object: a communication channel that every attention head and MLP reads from and writes to. Interpretability, logit lens, and steering vectors all depend on that view. It starts with the embedding layer.

1:00 INTUITION — Think of the residual stream as a shared whiteboard per token, 768 numbers wide. The embedding writes the first draft: what token is this, where is it. Each block reads the board, computes something, and adds its note. Nobody erases. The final layer reads the board and predicts. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — x_0 = W_E[idx] + W_P[pos], W_E (V, C), W_P (T_max, C). Block l: x_{l+1} = x_l + a_l + m_l where a_l = Attn(LN(x_l)), m_l = MLP(LN(x_l + a_l)). Unrolled: x_L = x_0 + sum_l (a_l + m_l). So the final stream is a sum of every component's output, which is why you can attribute logits to components linearly (up to the final LayerNorm's scale). Norm growth: if writes are roughly independent, ||x_l||^2 grows roughly linearly in l.

5:30 CODE — class Embeddings(nn.Module): __init__(V, T_max, C): self.wte = nn.Embedding(V, C); self.wpe = nn.Embedding(T_max, C). forward(idx (B,T)): pos = torch.arange(T, device=idx.device); return self.wte(idx) + self.wpe(pos), (B,T,C). Copy HF weights in: my.wte.weight.copy_(hf.transformer.wte.weight). For the stream: out = hf(idx, output_hidden_states=True); hs = out.hidden_states, a tuple of 13 tensors of (B,T,768). Compute hs[l].norm(dim=-1) per layer and position.

9:00 RECEIPT — torch.testing.assert_close(my_emb(idx), out.hidden_states[0]). Additivity check: register hooks on h[l].attn and h[l].mlp outputs and assert_close(hidden_states[l] + attn_out + mlp_out, hidden_states[l+1]) for l in 0..10. For l = 11 it fails on purpose: HF applies ln_f before storing the last hidden state.

10:30 MEASURE — Plot mean residual norm vs layer, 0 to 11, for 100 TinyStories sequences. Plot per-position norm at the last layer: position 0 stands out by a huge margin, and a few dimensions carry massive values. Logit lens: apply ln_f and W_E^T to each layer's stream and show the top token per layer for one sentence.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — The residual stream is a running sum; every block is a read-then-add, which makes the network decomposable. Interview line: because x_L = x_0 + sum of component outputs, you can attribute the final logits to individual heads and MLPs, which is the basis of circuits-style interpretability.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Positional information.
key_math: x_0 = W_E[idx] + W_P[pos];  x_{l+1} = x_l + a_l + m_l;  x_L = x_0 + sum_l (a_l + m_l);  logit lens: logits_l = LN_f(x_l) W_E^T

interview_q: What is the residual stream and why does it matter for interpretability? Answer: it is the per-token vector that every block reads from and adds to; since the final state is the embedding plus a sum of all head and MLP outputs, contributions to the logits can be decomposed and attributed to individual components.
explainer: Each token owns a 768 number vector. We call it the residual stream. Think of it as a shared whiteboard.
The embedding writes the first draft. What this token is, plus where it sits in the sentence.
Then block one reads the board, computes something, and adds its note on top. Nothing gets erased.
Every attention layer and every MLP in the model does exactly this. Read the board, compute something, add the result.
So the final vector is just the embedding plus the sum of every component's output.
Measure the stream's length at each layer. It keeps growing as block after block adds its note.
Decode the stream at every layer with the output matrix. You can watch the guess sharpen layer by layer.

hook: Shuffle the words of a sentence and attention without positions gives you the same answers, just shuffled. Here's the proof in one assert.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Shuffle the words and plain attention gives the exact same outputs, just shuffled. It has no idea what order they came in.

0:15 QUESTION — 'Dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' must mean different things, but self-attention is a weighted sum over a set. The 2017 transformer fixed this with sinusoidal position encodings, GPT-2 learned a 1024 by 768 table, and Llama uses RoPE, which we build in E15. First we prove the problem exists.

1:00 INTUITION — Attention compares every token with every other by dot product. Swap two tokens and you swap two rows and two columns of the score matrix; each output row is still the same weighted average, just in a new slot. So we stamp a position signature onto each token before attention: a pattern of sines and cosines at many frequencies, like the hands of a clock running at different speeds. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Equivariance: for a permutation matrix P, Attn(PX) = softmax(P X W_q W_k^T X^T P^T / sqrt(d)) P X W_v = P softmax(...) P^T P X W_v = P Attn(X), since softmax acts row-wise and P^T P = I. Sinusoidal: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^{2i/d}), PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^{2i/d}). Wavelengths form a geometric series from 2 pi to 10000 * 2 pi. Key property: for each frequency w_i, [sin(w(p+k)), cos(w(p+k))] is a fixed 2x2 rotation of [sin(wp), cos(wp)], so PE(p+k) is a linear function of PE(p) independent of p.

6:00 CODE — x = torch.randn(1, 8, 64); attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(64, 4, batch_first=True); perm = torch.randperm(8). out = attn(x, x, x, need_weights=False)[0]; outp = attn(x[:, perm], x[:, perm], x[:, perm], need_weights=False)[0]. def sinusoidal(T, d) -> (T, d): pos = torch.arange(T)[:, None]; div = torch.exp(torch.arange(0, d, 2) * (-math.log(10000.0) / d)); pe[:, 0::2] = sin(pos*div); pe[:, 1::2] = cos(pos*div). Add to x and rerun the shuffle test. Plot pe as a heatmap and GPT-2's learned wpe as a heatmap.

9:00 RECEIPT — Without positions: torch.testing.assert_close(outp, out[:, perm]). With sinusoidal positions added after shuffling tokens (positions stay in place): the same assert fails, max diff order 1. Rotation property: for k=5 build the block-diagonal rotation M_k from angles k*w_i and assert_close(pe[5:] , pe[:-5] @ M_k.T) at atol 1e-5. Formula check against The Annotated Transformer's PositionalEncoding with the same d: identical.

10:30 MEASURE — Heatmap of sinusoidal PE (positions x dims), the dot product PE(p) . PE(p+k) vs k (decays with distance), and the cosine-similarity matrix of GPT-2's learned wpe rows, which shows smooth banded structure that looks a lot like sinusoids.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Self-attention is permutation-equivariant, so order has to be injected; sinusoids make relative offsets a linear rotation. Interview line: attention without positions treats input as a set; that linear-shift property of sinusoids is the seed of RoPE.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Attention intuition: a soft dictionary lookup.
key_math: Attn(PX) = P Attn(X);  PE(p,2i) = sin(p/10000^{2i/d}), PE(p,2i+1) = cos(p/10000^{2i/d});  [sin w(p+k), cos w(p+k)] = R(wk) [sin wp, cos wp]

receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(attn(xp,xp,xp)[0], attn(x,x,x)[0][:, perm]) with xp = x[:, perm] and no positions; after adding sinusoidal(8, 64) the assert fails; assert_close(pe[k:], pe[:-k] @ M_k.T, atol=1e-5).
gotchas: Saying attention is permutation-invariant, it is equivariant (outputs permute with inputs) unless you pool; testing with a causal mask, which is itself position information and breaks the symmetry; interleaving sin/cos as [sin..., cos...] halves instead of even/odd indices and then failing to match the reference
interview_q: Why does a transformer need positional encodings? Answer: self-attention without positions is permutation-equivariant, so it cannot distinguish word orders; adding position information (sinusoidal, learned, or rotary) breaks the symmetry, and sinusoids have the property that a shift by k is a fixed linear map, which helps model relative positions.
explainer: Here is attention on four words with no position information. Each output is a weighted mix of all the words.
Now shuffle the words. Every output is identical, it just moved to the new slot.
That is because swapping two tokens swaps a row and a column of the score grid. Nothing else changes.
So we stamp each position with a signature, built from sine waves of many different speeds.
Fast waves tell nearby positions apart. Slow waves tell far apart positions apart. Like hands on a clock.
Here is the whole encoding as a picture. Positions down the side, dimensions across the top.
Moving forward by k positions is just a rotation of each sine and cosine pair. Same rotation everywhere.
GPT-2 learned its position table from scratch instead. Its learned table ends up looking surprisingly similar to sinusoids.

hook: Attention is a dictionary where every key partly matches. Turn up the sharpness and it becomes an exact lookup.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Attention is a Python dictionary where every key partly matches. Make it sharp enough and it becomes an exact lookup.

0:15 QUESTION — Queries, keys and values sound like jargon. They are the three roles every token plays in every attention head of every GPT, Claude and Llama model. If you can compute one attention output by hand on four tokens, the code in the next three episodes is just bookkeeping.

1:00 INTUITION — A dict lookup: compare your query with each key, return the value of the one that matches. Attention makes it soft: score every key by similarity with the query, turn scores into weights that sum to one, and return the weighted average of the values. Each token asks a question with its query, advertises itself with its key, and offers content with its value. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — For one query q in R^d and keys K (n, d), values V (n, d_v): scores s = K q / sqrt(d), weights a = softmax(s), output o = a^T V. Batched over queries: O = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V. Worked example, d = 2, four tokens: K = [[1,0],[0,1],[1,1],[-1,0]], V = [[10,0],[0,10],[5,5],[0,0]], q = [2,0]. Scores q.k = [2, 0, 2, -2], divided by sqrt 2 = [1.414, 0, 1.414, -1.414]. Softmax gives about [0.43, 0.10, 0.43, 0.03]. Output about [6.5, 3.2]. Scale q by 100: weights split 0.5/0.5 between keys 1 and 3 because they tie, output [7.5, 2.5]. Break the tie and it snaps to one value.

6:00 CODE — K = torch.tensor([[1.,0],[0,1],[1,1],[-1,0]]); V = torch.tensor([[10.,0],[0,10],[5,5],[0,0]]); q = torch.tensor([[2.,0]]). def soft_lookup(q (m,d), K (n,d), V (n,dv), temp=1.0) -> (m, dv): s = q @ K.T / math.sqrt(d) / temp; a = s.softmax(-1); return a @ V. Print a and the output. Then sweep temp from 10 down to 0.01 and print the weights. Then let Q, K, V come from learned projections of four embeddings x (4, 8): Q = x @ Wq, etc.

9:00 RECEIPT — Hand numbers first, written on screen before running. Then torch.testing.assert_close(soft_lookup(q, K, V), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q[None], K[None], V[None])[0]). Hard-lookup limit: with q = [2, -0.1] and temp=0.001, assert_close(output, V[0], atol=1e-4) since key 1 (score 2.0) now beats key 3 (score 1.9).
10:30 MEASURE — Bar chart of attention weights as temperature drops: uniform, soft, one-hot. Entropy of the weights vs temperature on a log axis.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Attention is a differentiable dictionary lookup: similarity, softmax, weighted average. Interview line: the softmax temperature, which is 1/sqrt(d) by default, controls how close attention is to an exact lookup.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Why divide by sqrt(d_k).
key_math: s = K q / sqrt(d);  a = softmax(s);  o = sum_i a_i v_i;  O = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V

interview_q: Explain queries, keys and values in one sentence each. Answer: the query is what a token is looking for, the key is what each token offers to be matched on, and the value is what it actually passes along; the output is the softmax-of-similarity weighted average of values.
explainer: A Python dictionary takes a key and returns exactly one value. Attention is a softer version of that.
Here are four keys, each a little arrow in two dimensions, and each with a value attached.
Our query is another arrow. We score each key by its dot product with the query.
Softmax turns those four scores into weights that are all positive and add up to exactly one.
The output is the weighted average of the values. Mostly values one and three, a bit of value two.
Turn the temperature down and the weights get sharper. At the extreme, one key wins outright.
In a real model, every token makes its own query, key and value from its embedding, with learned matrices.

hook: Remove one division from attention and at d equals 1024 the softmax turns almost one-hot at initialization. The fix is the square root of d.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Delete one division from attention and at d of 1024 the softmax is nearly one-hot before training starts. Gradients die.

0:15 QUESTION — The transformer paper gives the scaling one sentence. Interviewers ask for the full derivation, and the same variance argument drives init schemes and muP. We derive it, measure it, and show what PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention does by default.

1:00 INTUITION — A dot product is a sum of d terms. Add up more random terms and the total spreads out more. Wide spread scores mean one score towers over the rest, softmax gives it nearly all the weight, and a nearly one-hot softmax has nearly zero gradient. Dividing by sqrt(d) keeps the spread fixed as d grows. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Assume q_i, k_i independent, mean 0, variance 1. Then E[q_i k_i] = E[q_i]E[k_i] = 0 and Var(q_i k_i) = E[q_i^2] E[k_i^2] - 0 = 1. The terms are independent, so Var(q . k) = sum_i Var(q_i k_i) = d, std = sqrt(d). Therefore Var(q . k / sqrt(d)) = d / d = 1. Why saturation kills learning: the softmax Jacobian is J = diag(p) - p p^T. If p is one-hot, diag(p) = p p^T, so J = 0 and no gradient flows to the scores. Note muP argues for 1/d instead, because after training q and k become correlated and the dot product grows like d, not sqrt(d).

6:30 CODE — for d in [16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024]: q = torch.randn(100_000, d); k = torch.randn(100_000, d); s = (q*k).sum(-1); record s.var(). Saturation: q = torch.randn(1, d); K = torch.randn(64, d); p_raw = (q @ K.T).softmax(-1); p_scaled = (q @ K.T / d**0.5).softmax(-1); record p.max() and entropy -(p*p.log()).sum(). Gradient: s.requires_grad_(); loss = (p * torch.randn(64)).sum(); backward; record s.grad.norm() for raw vs scaled.

9:00 RECEIPT — Empirical variance within 2 percent of d for every d (100k samples), and scaled variance within 2 percent of 1. interview_q: Why does attention divide by sqrt(d_k)? Answer: with independent unit-variance entries, q.k has variance d_k, so scores grow with head size, the softmax saturates toward one-hot, and its Jacobian diag(p) - pp^T goes to zero; scaling by 1/sqrt(d_k) restores unit variance and healthy gradients.
explainer: A dot product adds up d little products. Each one is random, mean zero, variance one.
Add up more random terms and the total spreads out. With d terms, the variance is exactly d.
Wide scores are a problem for softmax. One score towers over the others and takes almost all the weight.
A nearly one hot softmax has nearly zero gradient. The scores, and everything feeding them, stop learning.
Divide by the square root of d and the variance is back to one, no matter how big d gets.
Measured. Raw variance climbs with slope one on a log log plot. Scaled variance stays flat at one.
PyTorch's scaled dot product attention does this by default. Its scale is one over root head size.

hook: Self-attention is five lines of PyTorch. Match PyTorch's fused kernel to float precision, then see why the fused kernel exists.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Self-attention is five lines of PyTorch. Mine matches PyTorch's fused kernel exactly. Then I'll show you why the fused kernel exists.

0:15 QUESTION — Every GPT block runs this. In production it runs inside FlashAttention or PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention, never as naive matmuls, because the T by T score matrix is huge. Writing the naive version and matching SDPA is step one toward our feather-attn project, a FlashAttention kernel in Triton.

1:00 INTUITION — Each token projects itself three ways: a query, a key and a value. Every query is dotted with every key, giving a T by T grid of scores. Softmax each row, then each row mixes the values. That is it. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — x (B, T, C). Q = x W_q, K = x W_k, V = x W_v with W (C, hs), so Q, K, V are (B, T, hs). S = Q K^T / sqrt(hs), (B, T, T). A = softmax(S, dim=-1), each row sums to 1. O = A V, (B, T, hs). FLOPs per forward: projections 3 * 2 B T C hs; QK^T 2 B T^2 hs; AV 2 B T^2 hs. Memory for S in fp32: 4 B T^2 bytes per head, at T = 8192 that is 256 MiB per head per sequence.

5:30 CODE — class Head(nn.Module): __init__(C, hs): self.q = nn.Linear(C, hs, bias=False); self.k, self.v likewise. forward(x): q, k, v = self.q(x), self.k(x), self.v(x), each (B,T,hs); att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) * hs**-0.5, (B,T,T); att = att.softmax(dim=-1); return att @ v, (B,T,hs). Test with B=4, T=128, C=256, hs=64, float32.

8:30 RECEIPT — q, k, v = head.q(x), head.k(x), head.v(x); torch.testing.assert_close(head(x), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)) at default float32 tolerances. Also in float64 with rtol=atol=1e-10 on CPU. Row sums: assert torch.allclose(att.sum(-1), torch.ones(B, T)). Gradient match: backward through both and assert_close on x.grad.

10:00 MEASURE — Time naive vs SDPA forward+backward for T in 512, 1024, 2048, 4096 with torch.utils.benchmark.Timer on the Mac (MPS) and, if available, a CUDA GPU. Peak memory vs T for the naive version: the T^2 curve. Note which SDPA backend is used on each device rather than assuming.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Self-attention is project, score, softmax, mix, and the naive form materializes a T^2 matrix that fused kernels avoid. Interview line: naive attention is O(T^2) in memory because of the score matrix; FlashAttention keeps the same FLOPs but tiles the computation so S never hits HBM.

interview_q: What are the time and memory complexity of self-attention, and how does FlashAttention change them? Answer: O(T^2 d) time and O(T^2) memory for the score matrix; FlashAttention keeps O(T^2 d) FLOPs but computes softmax in tiles with an online normalizer, so memory is O(T) and it is much faster because it avoids reading and writing S to HBM.
explainer: Here is our input. A batch of sequences, each token a vector of size C.
Three learned matrices project every token into a query, a key and a value of size hs.
Multiply queries by keys transposed. That gives a T by T grid of scores for every sequence.
Scale by one over root hs, then softmax along each row. Every row now sums to one.
Each row then mixes the values. The output has the same shape as the queries.
Our five lines of code match PyTorch's fused attention kernel, output for output, to float precision.
But that score grid grows with T squared. At eight thousand tokens it is enormous. That is why fused kernels exist.

hook: One line of code stops GPT from reading the answer. Get it slightly wrong and your training loss looks amazing and means nothing.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Forget one line and your GPT's training loss drops to almost zero. It's cheating. That line is the causal mask.

0:15 QUESTION — A decoder-only model like GPT predicts token t+1 from tokens up to t. During training we feed the whole sequence at once for efficiency, so something must stop position t from looking at t+1. That something is the causal mask, and it is also why the KV cache works at inference.

1:00 INTUITION — Draw the T by T score grid. Row i is query i, column j is key j. Everything above the diagonal is the future. Set those scores to minus infinity before softmax, and exp of minus infinity is exactly zero. Each row then averages only over the past and itself. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — M_ij = 0 if j <= i, -inf if j > i. A = softmax(QK^T/sqrt(hs) + M). For j > i, exp(-inf) = 0, so A_ij = 0 exactly and row i renormalizes over j <= i. Consequence: O_i depends only on x_1..x_i, so changing x_{i+1..T} cannot change O_i. Training on a length-T sequence gives T next-token predictions per forward pass. Causal attention does about half the useful work of full attention, T(T+1)/2 entries.

5:30 CODE — In Head.__init__: self.register_buffer('mask', torch.tril(torch.ones(T_max, T_max, dtype=torch.bool)), persistent=False). In forward: att = att.masked_fill(~self.mask[:T, :T], float('-inf')) before softmax. Alternative: pass is_causal=True to F.scaled_dot_product_attention. Leakage demo: train the tiny model on TinyStories windows with the mask removed and watch train loss fall far below the honest model's.

8:30 RECEIPT — torch.testing.assert_close(my_causal(q, k, v), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)). Zero future weight: assert (att.triu(diagonal=1) == 0).all(). Perturbation test: x2 = x.clone(); x2[:, t+1:] = torch.randn_like(x2[:, t+1:]); torch.testing.assert_close(head(x2)[:, :t+1], head(x)[:, :t+1]) for t = T//2.

10:00 MEASURE — Heatmap of one masked attention matrix, lower triangular. Loss curves: no-mask model racing toward a near-zero training loss vs the masked model, and the no-mask model's generations, which are garbage at inference.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — The causal mask sets future scores to minus infinity so softmax gives them exactly zero weight. Interview line: if your training loss looks too good, first check the mask and the x/y shift.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Multi-head attention.
key_math: M_ij = 0 (j<=i), -inf (j>i);  A = softmax(QK^T/sqrt(hs) + M);  A_ij = 0 for j>i;  O_i = f(x_1..x_i)

interview_q: How does a decoder-only transformer prevent information leakage from future tokens during training? Answer: a causal mask adds -inf to scores where key position > query position before softmax, making those weights exactly zero; this lets one forward pass produce T valid next-token predictions in parallel.
explainer: Here is the score grid. Rows are queries, columns are keys. Row three asks, which tokens should I look at?
Everything above the diagonal is a key from the future. Token three should not be able to see token five.
We add minus infinity to every future score. Then softmax turns exactly those into zeros.
Each row now averages only over itself and the past. The weights in each row still sum to one.
Proof. Scramble every token after position t. The outputs up to t do not change at all.
Remove the mask and the model just reads the answer. Training loss dives toward zero almost immediately.
But at generation time there is no future to read, so the cheater writes garbage.

hook: Multi-head attention is one big matmul, a reshape, and the same attention run twelve times in parallel. The reshape is where everyone gets it wrong.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Multi-head attention is the same attention twelve times in parallel. The hard part is a single reshape. Let's get it right.

0:15 QUESTION — GPT-2 small has 12 heads of size 64; Llama 3 8B has 32 query heads of size 128. One head can only compute one weighted average per token. Many heads let different positions be attended to for different reasons. PyTorch ships nn.MultiheadAttention, so we can test ours weight for weight.

1:00 INTUITION — Instead of one attention with width 768, cut the width into 12 slices of 64. Each slice is its own head with its own queries, keys and values, attending independently. Glue the 12 outputs back together and mix them with one output projection. Same parameter count as one big head, more expressive. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — C = nh * hs. qkv = x W_qkv + b, W_qkv (C, 3C), giving (B, T, 3C). Split to q, k, v each (B, T, C). Reshape (B, T, nh, hs) then transpose to (B, nh, T, hs). Attention per head: softmax(q k^T / sqrt(hs) + M) v, (B, nh, T, hs). Transpose back to (B, T, nh, hs), reshape to (B, T, C). out = y W_o + b_o, W_o (C, C). Params: 3C^2 + 3C + C^2 + C = 4C^2 + 4C = 2,362,368 for C = 768.

5:30 CODE — class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module): __init__(C, nh): self.c_attn = nn.Linear(C, 3*C); self.c_proj = nn.Linear(C, C). forward(x): B, T, C = x.shape; q, k, v = self.c_attn(x).split(C, dim=2); with einops: q = rearrange(q, 'b t (h d) -> b h t d', h=nh), same for k, v. y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True) or my causal attention; y = rearrange(y, 'b h t d -> b t (h d)'); return self.c_proj(y). Plain-PyTorch version: q.view(B, T, nh, hs).transpose(1, 2) and y.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, T, C).

8:30 RECEIPT — mha = nn.MultiheadAttention(C, nh, bias=True, batch_first=True). Copy weights: my.c_attn.weight.copy_(mha.in_proj_weight) (both (3C, C), rows ordered q, k, v), my.c_attn.bias.copy_(mha.in_proj_bias), my.c_proj.weight.copy_(mha.out_proj.weight), bias likewise. mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1) (True = blocked for MHA). torch.testing.assert_close(my(x), mha(x, x, x, attn_mask=mask, need_weights=False)[0]). Param count: assert sum(p.numel() for p in my.parameters()) == 4*C*C + 4*C.

10:00 MEASURE — Load GPT-2's layer 0 to 11 attention weights into my module and plot all 144 attention patterns on one sentence as a 12x12 grid of small heatmaps. Point out a previous-token head and heads that dump attention on position 0.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Multi-head attention is one fused QKV projection, a (B, T, C) to (B, nh, T, hs) reshape, parallel attention, and an output projection. Interview line: heads cost no extra parameters over one wide head; they trade per-head width for multiple independent attention patterns.

interview_q: Why use multiple attention heads instead of one big one? Answer: at the same parameter count, splitting C into nh heads gives nh independent softmax distributions per token, so the layer can attend to several positions for different reasons at once, such as previous token, syntactic head, and induction patterns.
explainer: One attention head gives each token a single weighted average. Sometimes a token needs to look at several things at once.
So we slice the 768 wide vectors into twelve slices of 64. Each slice becomes its own head.
One big matrix makes all the queries, keys and values at once. Then we split and reshape.
The reshape moves heads into their own dimension. B, T, C becomes B, heads, T, head size.
Now twelve separate attentions run in parallel, each one free to learn its own pattern over the sequence.
We glue the twelve head outputs back together and mix them with one shared output projection.
With the same weights copied in, our module matches PyTorch's own MultiheadAttention exactly, number for number.

hook: Attention gets the fame, but in GPT-2 the MLPs hold two thirds of every block's parameters. Here's what they're doing with them.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Attention gets the headlines. But two thirds of every GPT-2 block's parameters sit in the boring MLP. Let's see why.

0:15 QUESTION — Every transformer block since 2017 has a position-wise feed-forward network that expands 4x and contracts back. Research on factual recall, like Geva et al.'s key-value memory view and work on locating facts in GPT models, points at these layers as where a lot of knowledge lives. Here we build it, count it, and load GPT-2's real one.

1:00 INTUITION — Attention moves information between tokens. The MLP thinks about each token alone. Read W_in's rows as keys: each of 3072 hidden units fires when the residual stream matches its pattern. Read W_out's rows as values: each firing unit adds its own vector back to the stream. A soft lookup table with 3072 entries per layer. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — MLP(x) = W_out GELU(W_in x + b_in) + b_out, W_in (4C, C), W_out (C, 4C). Params: 4C^2 + 4C + 4C^2 + C = 8C^2 + 5C = 4,722,432 for C = 768. Attention: 4C^2 + 4C = 2,362,368. So MLP / (MLP + attention) = 2/3 ignoring biases and norms. Forward FLOPs per token: MLP 16C^2, attention projections 8C^2, attention scores and mixing 4TC. At C = 768 and T = 1024: 9.4M vs 4.7M vs 3.1M FLOPs per token per layer. Key-value view: MLP(x) = sum_i GELU(k_i . x + b_i) v_i.

6:00 CODE — class MLP(nn.Module): __init__(C): self.c_fc = nn.Linear(C, 4*C); self.c_proj = nn.Linear(4*C, C). forward(x (B,T,C)): return self.c_proj(F.gelu(self.c_fc(x), approximate='tanh')), with the hidden at (B,T,4C). Load GPT-2 layer 0: my.c_fc.weight.copy_(hf.transformer.h[0].mlp.c_fc.weight.T) because HF's Conv1D stores weights as (in, out); same for c_proj. count(module) helper.

9:00 RECEIPT — x = torch.randn(2, 16, 768); torch.testing.assert_close(my_mlp(x), hf.transformer.h[0].mlp(x)). Param assertion: assert count(my_mlp) == 8*768*768 + 5*768 == 4_722_432 and count(attn) == 2_362_368. Without the transpose, the copy either errors on shape or, for a square matrix like attention's c_proj, silently gives wrong outputs, show that.

10:30 MEASURE — Stacked bar of parameter share per block: MLP 66.6 percent, attention 33.3 percent, LayerNorms tiny. FLOPs share per token vs T: MLP dominates at short context, attention scores catch up as T grows past about 4C. Key-value probe: for one MLP neuron in a middle layer, list the top-activating tokens across 10k TinyStories tokens.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — The MLP is a per-token 4x-wide memory that holds most of the parameters and most of the FLOPs at normal context lengths. Interview line: attention cost grows with context length, MLP cost doesn't, so at short contexts the MLP dominates compute.

hook: Llama's MLP has three matrices, not two, and a hidden size of 8/3 the width. That fraction is a parameter budget.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Llama's MLP uses three matrices, not two, and a hidden size of eight thirds. That weird fraction is just accounting.

0:15 QUESTION — GPT-2 used GELU. Llama, Mistral, Qwen and most open models since use SwiGLU, from Shazeer's 2020 paper 'GLU Variants Improve Transformer'. Llama 2 7B's MLP hidden size is 11,008, not 4 x 4096 = 16,384. By the end you can derive that number.

1:00 INTUITION — ReLU is a hard gate: pass positive, kill negative. GELU is a soft version: multiply x by the probability that a standard normal is below x. A gated linear unit goes further: one projection decides how much to let through, a second projection decides what to let through, and you multiply them. A learned, input-dependent valve on every hidden unit. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — ReLU(x) = max(0, x). GELU(x) = x Phi(x), tanh approx 0.5 x (1 + tanh(sqrt(2/pi)(x + 0.044715 x^3))). SiLU(x) = Swish_1(x) = x sigmoid(x). FFN_SwiGLU(x) = W_2 (SiLU(W_1 x) * W_3 x), elementwise *, no biases. Param matching: standard FFN has 2 d (4d) = 8d^2. SwiGLU has 3 d h. Set 3dh = 8d^2, so h = 8d/3. For d = 768, h = 2048 exactly, and both are 4,718,592 weights. Llama 2 7B: 8 * 4096 / 3 = 10,922.67, rounded up to a multiple of 256 gives 11,008.

6:00 CODE — class FFN_GELU(d): c_fc Linear(d, 4d, bias=False), c_proj Linear(4d, d, bias=False). class FFN_ReLU same with F.relu. class SwiGLU(d, h=None): h = h or multiple_of_256(int(8*d/3)) or exactly 8*d//3 for the matched test; self.w1 = Linear(d, h, bias=False) (gate), self.w3 = Linear(d, h, bias=False) (up), self.w2 = Linear(h, d, bias=False) (down). forward(x (B,T,d)): return self.w2(F.silu(self.w1(x)) * self.w3(x)). Write my_gelu_tanh and my_silu by hand too.

explainer: Three activation functions. ReLU cuts negatives to zero. GELU does the same thing, but smoothly.
A gated unit uses two projections of the same input. One decides how much passes. The other decides what passes.
SwiGLU puts a SiLU on the gate, multiplies element by element, then projects back down.
That is three matrices instead of two. To keep the parameter count fair, we shrink the hidden size.
Two times four d squared equals three times d times h. Solve, and h is eight thirds of d.
For width 768 that is exactly 2048. Both versions have the same 4.7 million weights.
Llama 2's width is 4096. Eight thirds gives 10923, rounded up to a multiple of 256, gives 11008.

hook: RMSNorm deletes the mean from LayerNorm and nothing breaks. Llama, Mistral and Gemma all use it.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Take LayerNorm, delete the mean subtraction, delete the bias. That's RMSNorm. Most modern LLMs use it.

0:15 QUESTION — GPT-2 used LayerNorm. Llama, Mistral, Qwen and Gemma use RMSNorm, from Zhang and Sennrich 2019. PyTorch added torch.nn.RMSNorm in 2.4. Today we write it, match it, and measure whether it is actually cheaper on our hardware.

1:00 INTUITION — LayerNorm does two things: re-centers each token vector to mean zero and rescales it to unit spread. The RMSNorm paper's bet is that the rescaling is what matters for stable training, and re-centering is optional. Dropping it saves a reduction and a subtraction, and removes the bias. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — LayerNorm: y = (x - mu) / sqrt(sigma^2 + eps) * g + b, mu = mean(x), sigma^2 = mean((x - mu)^2). RMSNorm: y = x / sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) * g, no mean, no bias. Relation: RMS(x)^2 = sigma^2 + mu^2, so if mu = 0 the two are identical (when b = 0). RMSNorm is invariant to rescaling x by a positive constant, but not to shifting it. Gradient: one fewer reduction in forward and backward.

5:30 CODE — class RMSNorm(nn.Module): __init__(d, eps=1e-6): self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(d)). forward(x (B,T,d)): x32 = x.float(); y = x32 * torch.rsqrt(x32.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps); return (y * self.weight).to(x.dtype). Benchmark with torch.utils.benchmark.Timer: my RMSNorm, torch.nn.RMSNorm, nn.LayerNorm, at (8, 1024, 4096), on MPS and, if available, CUDA, both eager and torch.compile.

9:00 RECEIPT — ref = torch.nn.RMSNorm(4096, eps=1e-6); torch.testing.assert_close(my_rms(x), ref(x)). Production check: transformers LlamaRMSNorm(4096, eps=1e-6) with same weights, assert_close. Identity check: x0 = x - x.mean(-1, keepdim=True); assert_close(my_rms(x0), F.layer_norm(x0, (4096,), eps=1e-6), atol 1e-5). Scale invariance: assert_close(my_rms(3 * x), my_rms(x), atol 1e-5).

10:30 MEASURE — Timing table, LayerNorm vs RMSNorm, eager vs compiled, MPS vs CUDA. Be honest: these ops are memory-bound, so the speedup is often small once fused. Then a bf16 test: compute without the float32 upcast and show the error vs the fp32 reference growing.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — RMSNorm keeps LayerNorm's rescaling and drops re-centering and bias; it matches LayerNorm exactly on zero-mean input. Interview line: norms are memory-bound, so RMSNorm's real win is simplicity and a little bandwidth, and you still compute it in fp32 under bf16 training.

interview_q: What is the difference between LayerNorm and RMSNorm and why did Llama switch? Answer: RMSNorm divides by the root mean square without subtracting the mean and has no bias; it is simpler and slightly cheaper, and empirically trains as well, which is why Llama-family models use it.
explainer: LayerNorm does two jobs on each token. It moves the vector to mean zero, then scales it to unit size.
RMSNorm skips the first job entirely. There is no mean subtraction and no bias. It only rescales the vector.
It divides by the root mean square, the square root of the average of squared values.
If the vector already has mean zero, RMSNorm and LayerNorm give exactly the same answer.
Our version matches PyTorch's own RMSNorm. But watch the epsilon, because PyTorch's default is not Llama's.
Speed. Both are memory bound, so after fusion the gap is smaller than you might expect.

hook: Move the LayerNorm from after the residual add to before it and a transformer that diverged without warmup suddenly trains.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Same block, same weights, the LayerNorm moved one line up. One version diverges without warmup. The other trains fine.

0:15 QUESTION — The original 2017 transformer was post-norm. GPT-2 and nearly every LLM since are pre-norm. Xiong et al. 2020 showed why: post-norm has large gradients near the output at initialization and needs learning-rate warmup to survive. Today we assemble the block both ways and train them.

1:00 INTUITION — Post-norm normalizes after adding to the residual, so the residual stream itself is renormalized every layer and gradients must pass through every norm. Pre-norm normalizes only the copy going into each sublayer, so the residual stream is a clean highway from top to bottom, like M03's residual episode. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Post-norm: x = LN(x + Attn(x)); x = LN(x + MLP(x)). Pre-norm: x = x + Attn(LN1(x)); x = x + MLP(LN2(x)); plus a final LN_f before the head, since the stream is never normalized otherwise. In pre-norm, dx_L/dx_l = I + sum of sublayer Jacobian paths, so the identity path survives. In post-norm every layer's Jacobian goes through an LN Jacobian, and the gradient scale near the output is large at init (Xiong et al.), hence warmup.

5:30 CODE — class Block(nn.Module): __init__(C, nh, prenorm=True): self.ln_1 = nn.LayerNorm(C); self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(C, nh); self.ln_2 = nn.LayerNorm(C); self.mlp = MLP(C). forward(x (B,T,C)): if prenorm: x = x + self.attn(self.ln_1(x)); x = x + self.mlp(self.ln_2(x)); else: x = self.ln_1(x + self.attn(x)); x = self.ln_2(x + self.mlp(x)). Tiny LM: embeddings + 6 blocks (C=256, nh=8) + head, a 5-line random-window sampler over the M04 TinyStories .bin (proper loader in M06E01). AdamW lr 1e-3, no warmup vs 200-step warmup, 2k steps each.

9:00 RECEIPT — Production match: load GPT-2's layer 0 into my pre-norm Block (transpose Conv1D weights). out = hf.transformer.h[0](x); out = out[0] if isinstance(out, tuple) else out; torch.testing.assert_close(my_block(x), out, atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-5). This confirms GPT-2 is pre-norm. Training: pre-norm no-warmup reaches a lower val loss at 2k steps than post-norm no-warmup, which spikes or diverges; post-norm with warmup closes most of the gap.
10:30 MEASURE — Four loss curves: pre/post x warmup/no warmup. Per-layer gradient norms at step 0 for both: post-norm's grow toward the output layers, pre-norm's are flat.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Pre-norm keeps the residual stream un-normalized, so gradients have an identity path and training is stable without careful warmup. Interview line: pre-norm needs a final LayerNorm before the LM head, because nothing else normalizes the stream.
12:00 NEXT — Next: LM head and weight tying.

interview_q: Pre-norm or post-norm, and why? Answer: modern LLMs use pre-norm, x + F(LN(x)), because the residual path stays an identity so gradients are well-scaled at init and training is stable without long warmup; post-norm can reach slightly better quality when it trains, but is fragile at depth.
explainer: Two ways to build the same block. The only difference is where the LayerNorm sits.
Post norm adds first, then normalizes. The main road itself gets normalized at every layer.
Pre norm normalizes only the copy going into attention or the MLP. The main road stays untouched.
That untouched road is an identity path. Gradients flow straight from the loss to every layer.
Train both versions with no warmup. Post norm spikes and stalls. Pre norm trains smoothly from the start.
Give post norm a warmup and it recovers. That is why the original transformer needed one.
Load GPT-2's first block into our pre norm version. Outputs match exactly. GPT-2 is pre norm.

hook: GPT-2 uses one 38.6 million number matrix to read words in and write words out. Tying makes it 24 percent smaller.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — GPT-2 reads tokens and writes tokens with the same 38.6 million number matrix. Untie it and the model grows to 163 million.

0:15 QUESTION — The LM head turns the final hidden state into 50,257 logits. GPT-2 ties it to the input embedding, following Press and Wolf 2016. Small modern models like Llama 3.2 1B still tie; Llama 3 8B does not. Knowing the trade, and the bugs it causes when loading and saving, matters.

1:00 INTUITION — The embedding maps token to vector. The head scores a vector against every token. If a vector is close to token 'cat's embedding, it should score high for 'cat'. So use the same table both ways: the logit for token v is the dot product of the hidden state with v's embedding row. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Untied: logits = h W_U^T with W_U (V, C), separate from W_E (V, C). Tied: logits = h W_E^T. Shapes: h (B, T, C) times (C, V) gives (B, T, V). Savings: V C = 50,257 * 768 = 38,597,376. GPT-2 small: 124,439,808 tied vs 163,037,184 untied, a 23.7 percent reduction. Gradient: W_E now gets gradient from two places, the input lookup (sparse) and the output projection (dense over all V rows). Llama 3 8B untied head: 128,256 * 4096 = 525,336,576 params.

5:30 CODE — class GPT: self.wte = nn.Embedding(V, C); self.lm_head = nn.Linear(C, V, bias=False); self.lm_head.weight = self.wte.weight (assignment shares the Parameter, nanoGPT style). forward: logits = self.lm_head(self.ln_f(x)), equivalently F.linear(h, self.wte.weight). count_params(model) via model.parameters() (dedups shared) vs via state_dict() (does not). Inference trick: only compute logits for the last position, x[:, [-1], :], during generation.

8:30 RECEIPT — assert model.lm_head.weight is model.wte.weight and hf.lm_head.weight.data_ptr() == hf.transformer.wte.weight.data_ptr() for GPT2LMHeadModel. assert sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) == 124_439_808; untied copy == 163_037_184. Gradient check: after a backward, wte.weight.grad equals the sum of the grads you get by running an untied model with both matrices initialized equal, assert_close(tied_grad, untied_E_grad + untied_U_grad).

10:00 MEASURE — Param share bar: embedding/head as a fraction of total for GPT-2 small (31 percent tied), GPT-2 XL, Llama 3.2 1B (tied), Llama 3 8B (untied, two matrices of 525M). The fraction shrinks as models grow, which is why big models stop bothering.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Weight tying reuses W_E as the output projection, saving V*C parameters, which matters most for small models with big vocabularies. Interview line: tie after initialization, and remember state_dict lists the shared tensor twice while parameters() lists it once.
12:00 NEXT — Next: A full GPT in 150 lines.

interview_q: What is weight tying and when would you not use it? Answer: using the input embedding matrix as the output projection, logits = h E^T, which saves V*d parameters and often helps small models; large models often untie because the embedding is a small fraction of parameters and separate input and output representations add capacity.
explainer: At the bottom, the embedding table turns a token id into a vector. Fifty thousand rows, 768 numbers each.
At the top, the head must score a vector against every token in the vocabulary.
Scoring by dot product with each token's own embedding is a natural choice. Similar vectors, high score.
So we reuse the same table. Logits are the hidden state times the embedding matrix transposed.
Tying saves 38.6 million parameters. GPT-2 drops from 163 million parameters down to 124 million.
The shared table now learns from both ends. Its gradient is the sum of the two uses.

hook: RoPE rotates each query and key by an angle set by its position. The dot product then sees only the distance between them.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Rotate every query and key by an angle set by its position. Their dot product then only knows how far apart they are.

0:15 QUESTION — Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma and DeepSeek all use rotary position embeddings, from the RoFormer paper. Long-context tricks like changing the base, Llama 3 uses 500,000, and YaRN all work by editing RoPE. It is also the piece the DeepSeek-in-miniature project has to handle carefully with MLA.

1:00 INTUITION — Pair up the dimensions of a head: (0,1), (2,3), and so on. Treat each pair as an arrow in a plane. At position m, rotate pair i by angle m times theta_i. Two rotated arrows have a dot product that depends only on the angle between them, and that angle is (m - n) theta_i. Absolute positions cancel; relative position remains. Fast-spinning pairs see local detail, slow ones see long range. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — theta_i = base^{-2i/d}, i = 0..d/2 - 1, base = 10000, d = head size. Rotation for pair i at position m: [x'_{2i}, x'_{2i+1}] = [x_{2i} cos(m theta_i) - x_{2i+1} sin(m theta_i), x_{2i} sin(m theta_i) + x_{2i+1} cos(m theta_i)]. Complex view: z_i = x_{2i} + j x_{2i+1}, z'_i = z_i e^{j m theta_i}. Score: <R_m q, R_n k> = Re sum_i q_i conj(k_i) e^{j (m - n) theta_i}, a function of m - n only. Equivalently R_m^T R_n = R_{n-m}. Rotations preserve norms. Applied to q and k after projection, per head, never to v.

6:30 CODE — def rope_cache(T, hs, base=10000.0) -> (cos, sin) each (T, hs/2): inv_freq = 1.0 / base ** (torch.arange(0, hs, 2).float() / hs); ang = torch.outer(torch.arange(T).float(), inv_freq). def apply_rope_interleaved(x (B,nh,T,hs), cos, sin): x1, x2 = x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]; out = stack([x1*cos - x2*sin, x1*sin + x2*cos], -1).flatten(-2). def apply_rope_half(x, cos, sin): x1, x2 = x[..., :hs/2], x[..., hs/2:]; cat([x1*cos - x2*sin, x1*sin + x2*cos], -1), the GPT-NeoX/HF convention. Complex version with torch.polar and torch.view_as_complex for comparison. Insert into CausalSelfAttention after splitting heads; delete wpe.

9:30 RECEIPT — Relative property: for random q, k (hs = 64) and shift s = 7: torch.testing.assert_close(dot(rope(q, m), rope(k, n)), dot(rope(q, m + s), rope(k, n + s)), atol 1e-5) over many (m, n). Norms: assert_close(rope(x).norm(dim=-1), x.norm(dim=-1)). Production: build cos, sin from transformers LlamaRotaryEmbedding for a small LlamaConfig, apply apply_rotary_pos_emb from transformers.models.llama.modeling_llama, and assert_close against my apply_rope_half (check the signatures in your installed version). Interleaved equals half-split after permuting the head dims: assert_close.

11:00 MEASURE — Wavelengths 2 pi / theta_i on a log axis, from 6.3 to about 54,000 tokens for base 10000, hs = 64. Score vs relative distance for q = k = all-ones, showing the long-range decay the paper describes. Short TinyStories run: learned absolute positions vs RoPE at equal steps.

12:15 TAKEAWAY — RoPE rotates query and key pairs by position-dependent angles so attention scores depend only on relative position. Interview line: it adds no parameters, preserves norms, and context extension works by rescaling its frequencies, which is what changing the base does.
12:45 NEXT — Next: Counting parameters and FLOPs.

code_task: rope.py: rope_cache(T, hs, base=10000.0) -> cos, sin (T, hs/2); apply_rope_interleaved(x (B,nh,T,hs), cos, sin) and apply_rope_half(x, cos, sin) -> (B,nh,T,hs); complex-number version with torch.polar; RoPE-enabled CausalSelfAttention without wpe.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(score(rope(q,m), rope(k,n)), score(rope(q,m+7), rope(k,n+7)), atol=1e-5); norms preserved; my apply_rope_half matches transformers apply_rotary_pos_emb with LlamaRotaryEmbedding cos/sin; interleaved == half-split after head-dim permutation.
gotchas: Mixing conventions: Meta's reference rotates interleaved pairs (0,1),(2,3), HF/GPT-NeoX rotates (i, i+d/2), and loading weights across them needs a permutation of q/k projection rows; applying RoPE to v or to x before the head split; building angles in bf16, which loses precision at large positions, compute cos/sin in float32
interview_q: How does RoPE encode relative position, and why is it preferred over learned absolute embeddings? Answer: it rotates each 2D pair of query and key dimensions by m*theta_i, so their dot product depends only on m - n; it adds no parameters, preserves norms, and its frequencies can be rescaled for context extension.
explainer: Take a query vector and pair up its dimensions. Each pair is an arrow in a little 2D plane.
At position m, we rotate every pair by m times its own angle. Some pairs spin fast, some barely move.
Do the same to the keys. Now take the dot product of a rotated query and a rotated key.
A dot product only cares about the angle between two arrows. Here that angle is m minus n times theta.
Shift both positions by seven. Both arrows turn together, and the score does not change at all.
In complex numbers it is one line. Multiply each pair by e to the i m theta.
The angles form a geometric series. Fast pairs see nearby words, slow pairs see thousands of tokens away.
No parameters, and vector norms are unchanged. And our version matches Hugging Face's Llama rotary code exactly.

hook: Training compute is 6 times parameters times tokens. Here's where the 6 comes from, and a FLOP counter that agrees with my formula exactly.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Training compute is six times parameters times tokens. Where does the six come from? And can we prove it with a counter?

0:15 QUESTION — Every scaling law, every compute budget and every MFU number starts here. Kaplan et al. and Chinchilla use C = 6ND. CS336 makes you count it by hand. If you can do this for GPT-2 on a whiteboard, you can estimate any training run's cost in your head.

1:00 INTUITION — A matrix multiply of an (m, k) by a (k, n) matrix does m k n multiply-adds, which is 2mkn FLOPs. Every parameter in a linear layer is used once per token in a multiply-add: 2 FLOPs per parameter per token forward. Backward has to compute two things, the gradient for the input and the gradient for the weight, so it costs twice the forward. 2 + 4 = 6. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Params per layer: attention 4C^2 (q, k, v, o), MLP 8C^2, total 12C^2 (plus 13C of biases and norms). Model: N approx 12 L C^2 + V C. GPT-2 small: 12 * 12 * 768^2 = 84,934,656 vs exact non-embedding 85,054,464. Forward FLOPs per token: 2N_matmul + attention scores and mixing 4 T C per layer (2TC for QK^T, 2TC for AV, no causal savings). Training: C_train approx 6 N D, plus 3 * 4 L T C per token for attention, which Kaplan writes as 2 n_layer n_ctx d per token forward. For GPT-2 small on 10B tokens: 6 * 124e6 * 1e10 = 7.4e18 FLOPs; one H100 at 989 dense bf16 TFLOP/s and 40 percent MFU gives about 5.2 hours.

6:00 CODE — flops.py: def forward_flops(cfg, B, T) -> int: L, C, V = ...; matmul = 2 * B * T * (12 * L * C * C + V * C); attn = 4 * B * T * T * C * L; return matmul + attn. Count against: from torch.utils.flop_counter import FlopCounterMode; with FlopCounterMode(display=False) as fc: logits = model(idx); fwd = fc.get_total_flops(). Use my naive matmul attention (not SDPA) so every op is a plain matmul. Then a second counter around loss.backward().

9:00 RECEIPT — For the GPT-2 config with B = 1, T = 1024: assert fc_forward == forward_flops(cfg, 1, 1024) exactly (about 2.9e11; embedding lookups, softmax, GELU and norms are not counted by FlopCounterMode, and not by the formula). assert fc_backward == 2 * fc_forward. Then (fwd + bwd) / (B T) / N_matmul is about 6 plus the attention term, printed.

10:30 MEASURE — Stacked bar of FLOPs per token by component (QKV, attn scores, attn out, MLP, LM head) at T = 1024 and T = 8192: attention's share grows with T. Table: 6ND compute for GPT-2 small, Chinchilla-optimal D = 20N, and estimated H100-hours at 40 percent MFU.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Forward is 2 FLOPs per parameter per token, backward is 4, so training is about 6ND plus an attention term that grows with context. Interview line: estimate any training run's cost as 6 * params * tokens divided by (peak FLOP/s times MFU).
12:00 NEXT — Next: Memory accounting for training.

receipt: with FlopCounterMode(display=False) as fc: model(idx) for GPT-2 config, B=1, T=1024; assert fc.get_total_flops() == forward_flops(cfg, 1, 1024); backward counter == 2 * forward exactly.
gotchas: Counting a multiply-add as 1 FLOP and getting half of everyone else's numbers; including embedding parameters in N for the 2N forward rule, a lookup does no matmul (the tied head does count); using SDPA under the counter and getting attention counted differently, use explicit matmuls when checking the formula
interview_q: Estimate the FLOPs to train a 7B model on 2T tokens and how long it takes on 1,024 H100s. Answer: 6 * 7e9 * 2e12 = 8.4e22 FLOPs; at 989 TFLOP/s and 40 percent MFU per GPU, that is about 4e14 * 1024 = 4.05e17 FLOP/s, so about 2.1e5 seconds, roughly 2.4 days.
explainer: A matrix multiply of m by k times k by n does m k n multiply adds. That is two m k n FLOPs.
In a linear layer, each weight is used once per token, for one multiply and one add.
So the forward pass costs about two FLOPs for every parameter, for every token we process.
Backward computes two gradients for each layer, one for the input and one for the weights. Twice the work.
Two plus four is six. So training costs six times the parameters times the number of tokens.
Attention adds a term that grows with context length, because every token compares with every other.
PyTorch's own FLOP counter agrees with our formula. Not approximately. Exactly, down to the last FLOP.

hook: Training GPT-2 small needs about 2 GB just for weights, gradients and Adam, before a single activation. Predict the peak, then measure it.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Before one activation is stored, training GPT-2 small already needs about two gigabytes. Let's predict the peak, then measure it.

0:15 QUESTION — Out-of-memory is the most common training failure. ZeRO, FSDP, activation checkpointing and mixed precision all exist to attack one line of this ledger. The 4D-parallel training project needs this ledger per GPU, so we build it on one model first and check every line.

1:00 INTUITION — Four buckets. Weights. Gradients, same size as weights. Adam's two running averages, twice the size of the weights. And activations: every tensor the forward pass saves so backward can use it, which grows with batch size and sequence length and is often the biggest bucket. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — fp32 AdamW: params 4N + grads 4N + Adam m and v 8N = 16N bytes. GPT-2 small: 16 * 124.4M = 1.99 GB. Mixed precision (bf16 compute, fp32 master): bf16 params 2N + grads 2N + fp32 master 4N + Adam 8N = 16N still, which is why ZeRO shards it. Activations per layer scale as B * T * C * (a constant from the saved tensors) plus B * nh * T^2 for attention scores when not using a fused kernel. Korthikanti et al. 2022 give s b h (34 + 5 a s / h) bytes per layer for 16-bit training with dropout; we derive our own constant for our exact code.

6:00 CODE — ledger(model, B, T) -> dict with params, grads, adam, activations predicted bytes. Measure static buckets exactly: sum(p.numel() * p.element_size()), after one optimizer.step() sum of nbytes over optimizer.state[p]['exp_avg'] and ['exp_avg_sq']. Measure activations exactly with torch.autograd.graph.saved_tensors_hooks(pack, unpack), where pack records t.untyped_storage().data_ptr() and nbytes, deduplicated by storage. On CUDA also read torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated(); on Mac, torch.mps.current_allocated_memory() at checkpoints.

9:00 RECEIPT — assert param_bytes == 4 * 124_439_808; assert adam_bytes == 8 * 124_439_808 after one step. Activations: predicted vs saved-tensor total within 5 percent for B in {1, 4, 8}, T in {256, 512, 1024}, naive attention and SDPA. On CUDA: predicted static + activations + logits within about 10 percent of torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated().

10:30 MEASURE — Stacked bar ledger per config. Activation bytes vs T: linear with fused attention, quadratic with naive attention. The logits bucket: B * T * 50257 * 4 bytes is 206 MB at B=1, T=1024, and its gradient doubles it, a surprise to most people. Then turn on activation checkpointing per block (torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint) and show the activation bar shrink.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Training memory is 16 bytes per parameter for weights, grads and Adam, plus activations that scale with B, T and L. Interview line: at 16N, a 7B model needs about 112 GB before activations, which is why you shard optimizer state with ZeRO or FSDP.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Multi-query and grouped-query attention.
key_math: static = 4N (params) + 4N (grads) + 8N (Adam m,v) = 16N bytes;  activations ~ L B T C k + L B nh T^2 (unfused);  logits = 4 B T V bytes

gotchas: Counting saved tensors twice when views share storage, dedupe by storage pointer; forgetting Adam state is created lazily on the first step, so memory jumps after step 1; ignoring the logits and their gradient, which at a 50k vocab can rival the whole model's activations
interview_q: How much GPU memory does it take to train a 7B model with AdamW in mixed precision? Answer: about 16 bytes per parameter for bf16 weights and grads, fp32 master weights and two fp32 Adam moments, so roughly 112 GB before activations; activations add a term proportional to batch, sequence length, layers and width, reduced by activation checkpointing.
explainer: Training memory comes in four buckets. Let's fill them one at a time for GPT-2 small.
Weights first. 124 million parameters at four bytes each comes to about half a gigabyte.
Gradients are exactly the same size as the weights. That is another half gigabyte gone.
Adam keeps two running averages for every parameter. That is twice the weights, another full gigabyte.
Then activations. Everything the forward pass saves for backward. It grows with batch and sequence length.
Even the output logits are big. Fifty thousand scores for every token, plus a gradient of the same size.
We predict every bucket, then measure each one exactly by hooking saved tensors. They agree.
Checkpointing trades compute for memory. Recompute the activations during backward and that bin shrinks a lot.

hook: Llama 2 70B shares each key-value head across 8 query heads. Its KV cache drops from 2.5 MB to 320 KB per token.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Llama 2 70B shares each key-value head across eight query heads. Its KV cache drops from 2.5 megabytes per token to 320 kilobytes.

0:15 QUESTION — At inference, every generated token reads the cached keys and values of every previous token. That cache, not the weights, limits batch size and context length in serving. Shazeer's multi-query attention and Ainslie et al.'s grouped-query attention shrink it; Llama 2 70B, Llama 3 and Mistral use GQA. It sets up the featherserve inference project and DeepSeek's MLA later.

1:00 INTUITION — In multi-head attention every query head has its own key and value head. In multi-query attention, all query heads share one key-value head. Grouped-query sits in between: query heads are split into groups, and each group shares one key-value head. Queries keep their diversity; the cache shrinks by the group size. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — nh query heads, n_kv key-value heads, g = nh / n_kv. q (B, nh, T, hs); k, v (B, n_kv, T, hs). Expand k, v by repeating each head g times along dim 1 to (B, nh, T, hs), then ordinary attention. KV cache bytes per token = 2 (K and V) * L * n_kv * hs * bytes_per_elem. Llama 2 70B: L = 80, nh = 64, n_kv = 8, hs = 128, fp16: 2 * 80 * 8 * 128 * 2 = 327,680 bytes = 320 KiB; with full MHA (n_kv = 64) it would be 2.5 MiB. At 4096 tokens per sequence: 1.25 GiB vs 10 GiB. Projection params: W_k, W_v shrink from C x C to C x (n_kv hs). Uptraining: initialize a GQA checkpoint by mean-pooling the original heads in each group.

6:00 CODE — class GQA(nn.Module): __init__(C, nh, n_kv): hs = C // nh; self.wq = nn.Linear(C, nh*hs, bias=False); self.wk = nn.Linear(C, n_kv*hs, bias=False); self.wv likewise; self.wo = nn.Linear(nh*hs, C, bias=False). forward(x): q (B,nh,T,hs), k, v (B,n_kv,T,hs); k = k.repeat_interleave(nh // n_kv, dim=1); v likewise; y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True); y (B,T,C) -> wo. Variant without materializing the repeat: pass enable_gqa=True to SDPA (PyTorch 2.5+). kv_cache_bytes(L, n_kv, hs, dtype_bytes, T) helper. mean_pool_heads(wk_mha, nh, n_kv) for uptraining.

9:00 RECEIPT — torch.testing.assert_close(gqa(x), reference) where reference = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True, enable_gqa=True) on the unexpanded k, v. Special cases: n_kv = nh reproduces my E08 MHA with the same weights (assert_close); n_kv = 1 is MQA. Cache table: assert kv_cache_bytes(80, 8, 128, 2, 1) == 327_680 and kv_cache_bytes(80, 64, 128, 2, 1) == 2_621_440. Cross-check config numbers against transformers' LlamaConfig num_key_value_heads for a public Llama-architecture model.

10:30 MEASURE — KV cache table per token and at 8k context for GPT-2 small (MHA, 36 KiB/token fp16), Llama 2 7B (MHA), Llama 2 70B (GQA-8), Llama 3 8B (GQA-8, 128 KiB/token), Mistral 7B. Max batch size that fits next to the weights on an 80 GB GPU for each. Decode-step latency on the Mac for nh=32 with n_kv in {32, 8, 1} at long context.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — GQA shares each key-value head across a group of query heads, cutting KV cache and memory bandwidth by the group size with little quality loss. Interview line: decoding is memory-bandwidth bound on reading the KV cache, so shrinking n_kv speeds up generation and raises the batch size you can serve.
12:00 NEXT — Next: The data loader for LM pretraining.

gotchas: Using repeat instead of repeat_interleave, which orders heads h0,h1,h0,h1 instead of h0,h0,h1,h1 and pairs queries with the wrong KV head; forgetting that enable_gqa needs PyTorch 2.5 or newer; computing cache size per layer and forgetting the factor of 2 for K and V or the number of layers
interview_q: Why does grouped-query attention speed up inference? Answer: autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth bound on reading the KV cache; with n_kv shared key-value heads instead of nh, the cache and its reads shrink by nh/n_kv, allowing longer contexts and larger batches with little quality loss compared to MHA.
explainer: In multi head attention, every query head brings its own key head and value head. Thirty two of each.
At inference we must store every key and value for every past token. That is the KV cache.
Multi query attention goes to the extreme. All query heads share one single key and value head.
Grouped query attention is the middle. Query heads form groups, and each group shares one key value head.
In code, we repeat each key value head across its group, then run ordinary attention.
The cache shrinks by the group size. For Llama 2 70B, from 2.5 megabytes per token to 320 kilobytes.
Smaller cache means more sequences fit on the GPU, and each decode step reads less memory.
